Call recap:
- Primary use case: customer support agent assist (summarization + reranking) and embed-based semantic search across product docs.
- Expected steady QPS: ~25 requests/s (batchable embedding calls), peak/spike traffic for live events ~120–150 req/s for generation/rerank.
- Architecture: serverless frontend (AWS Lambda) that fans out to a backend pool; need low-latency generation for chat and async batch for embeddings.

Integration/architecture items we discussed:
- SDK setup & auth: recommend Redwood SDK server-side with API key stored in KMS; for serverless, use short-lived credentials where possible or a proxy microservice to avoid leaking keys.
- Routing: route generation requests to low-latency region; route bulk embedding jobs to cheaper throughput nodes.
- Structured output / tool calling: use the SDK's structured-output mode to enforce JSON schema + function/tool-calling hooks for external action.
- Embeddings & rerankers: batch embeddings to 256–512 vectors per request where possible; use in-memory cache for top-K to reduce calls.
- Rate limiting & retries: client-side rate limiting + exponential backoff recommended; idempotency keys for non-idempotent ops (see below).

2) Any strict SLA/latency target for the chat path (p50/p95)?
3) Do you have any restrictions around header propagation (X-Request-ID / Idempotency-Key)?

Thanks Priya — diagram received and really helpful. Answering your two asks and adding recommended patterns we use with customers in serverless architectures.

Canonical request IDs / idempotency:
- Recommended headers: X-Request-ID (UUID v4) for observability and tracing; Idempotency-Key (UUID or opaque deterministic id) for de-duplicating non-idempotent operations (e.g., create-ticket, accept-payment).
- Pattern: generate X-Request-ID at the edge (client/balancer) for every request. For user-triggered actions that must be idempotent, bus the same Idempotency-Key for retries originating from the same logical action.
- For serverless retries where the caller might not be able to persist keys, use a short-lived dedupe window on our side (e.g., 30s) keyed by X-Request-ID + client_id.

429 / Retry / Backoff guidance:
- Treat 429 as retryable; first check for a Retry-After header from Redwood. If present, respect it.
- Recommended client backoff: exponential with full jitter (see: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/). Example starting values:
  * base: 200ms
  * multiplier: 2
  * max_backoff: 10s
  * max_retries: 5 (for interactive generation); for async batch/embeddings you can allow more retries (8–10) with longer total timeout.
- For 5xx: use similar backoff but prefer slightly longer base (500ms) and fewer retries if operation is not idempotent.
- If you see sustained 429s at your peak, consider client-side token-bucket rate limiting to smooth bursts and prevent retry storms.

Batching & embeddings:
- For embeddings, batch 128–512 ids depending on vector size; prefer async job submission with retryable job status checks vs synchronous long-running requests.
- For rerankers, consider a two-step approach: candidate retrieval (cheap) -> rerank (expensive) with caching of top candidates per query.

Headers & sample checklist:
- Required: Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY> (server-side only)
- Recommended: X-Request-ID: <uuid4>, Idempotency-Key: <uuid-or-deterministic>, X-Client-Region: <region-id>
